title: CLARITY Act Q&A: Why Crypto Market Structure Can't Wait
gist: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon argue the CLARITY Act (HR 3633) would finish the job the GENIUS Act started by giving the SEC/CFTC a permanent, risk-based framework for crypto markets — and that regulatory ambiguity, not regulation itself, is what currently rewards offshore bad actors and pushes U.S. builders overseas.

themes.theme: Why crypto now needs federal market-structure rules

insights.claim: Stablecoins have grown to rival the Visa network in scale, with trillions of dollars transacted, while transaction costs on widely used blockchains have fallen from several dollars to under a penny with settlement in under a second.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Scale has outrun regulatory infrastructure; investors should expect market-structure legislation to become a forcing function rather than a nice-to-have as stablecoin volumes approach payment-network scale.
insights.quote: stablecoins now rival the size of the Visa network, with trillions of dollars transacted
insights.locator: A technology has become an industry

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act (law since July 2025) regulated stablecoins but left the underlying blockchain networks and broader crypto markets without a comprehensive federal structure, which the authors compare to regulating cell phones while leaving cell towers unregulated.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Investors in stablecoin-adjacent infrastructure and exchanges should watch CLARITY as the second, necessary leg of the regulatory stool — GENIUS alone doesn't de-risk the sector.
insights.quote: It is the equivalent of regulating cell phones while leaving the cell towers in legal limbo.
insights.locator: The GENIUS Act, which became law in July 2025

insights.claim: Agency guidance is an inadequate substitute for legislation because it can be reversed with a change in agency leadership or administration, creating multi-year planning risk for companies building products with 5-10 year horizons.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Legal/regulatory risk in crypto is a durable discount on long-horizon crypto infrastructure investment until statute (not guidance) exists; a passed CLARITY Act would be a re-rating catalyst.
insights.locator: Agency guidance can fill some gaps

insights.claim: Crypto exchanges currently lack the market-wide federal system of registration, supervision, audits, disclosures, surveillance, and customer-asset protection that NYSE and Nasdaq operate under.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Exchange-listed or exchange-adjacent crypto equities/tokens carry a structural governance discount versus traditional exchanges until CLARITY-style oversight is enacted.
insights.locator: The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq have federal regulators

insights.claim: CLARITY would create a pathway for digital assets to move from SEC to CFTC oversight, requiring federally registered exchanges to undergo audits, safeguard customer assets, and comply with anti-fraud and insider-trading rules, with noncompliant firms barred from operating in the U.S.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Watch for CFTC-registered exchange status as a compliance moat that could favor incumbent, well-capitalized U.S. exchanges over unregistered offshore competitors.
insights.locator: A federally registered crypto exchange would be subject to audits

insights.claim: The authors cite FTX's alleged commingling of funds among related entities and failure to hold claimed customer assets, and Terra-Luna's collapse as a stablecoin that was not actually backed by reserves, as the specific failure modes CLARITY-style audits and reserve requirements are designed to prevent.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Due diligence on any crypto platform should specifically check for the FTX pattern (commingled entities, unverified reserves) and the Terra-Luna pattern (unbacked stability claims) as CLARITY's core enforcement targets.
insights.quote: FTX allegedly moved money among related entities, lacked adequate controls, and did not hold the customer assets it claimed to hold.
insights.locator: Those requirements help prevent the conditions that allowed FTX

themes.theme: Regulatory ambiguity as a competitive distortion

insights.claim: Regulatory ambiguity creates a race to the bottom: compliant U.S. companies bear heavy costs (lawyers, controls, audits, sanctions screening) while offshore competitors avoid those costs, copy products, undercut on fees, and move faster.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Compliance-cost asymmetry is a structural headwind for U.S.-domiciled crypto platforms competing against offshore rivals; a CLARITY-style perimeter would reprice that disadvantage by constraining offshore access to U.S. users.
insights.quote: A noncompliant offshore exchange shouldn’t be able to serve Americans while a compliant U.S. exchange bears the full cost of following the law.
insights.locator: Regulatory ambiguity creates a race to the bottom.

insights.claim: CLARITY would define the regulatory perimeter (which businesses are intermediaries, which rules apply, which agency supervises) and subject firms holding customer funds to the same AML, sanctions, and Treasury requirements as payment providers and fintechs.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Expect crypto intermediaries to be pulled into the same AML/sanctions compliance stack as fintech payment processors, raising the bar to entry but reducing tail regulatory risk for compliant players.
insights.quote: Clear rules favor companies willing to meet a standard. Gray areas favor companies willing to exploit them.
insights.locator: CLARITY would define the regulatory perimeter

insights.claim: Public blockchains are highly transparent rather than anonymous: transactions are permanently recorded and investigators can trace fund movement to exchanges, accounts, and devices even years later, a property some national security officials call creating 'prosecution futures.'
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: The permanent-ledger property differentiates crypto from cash for law enforcement purposes and undercuts the narrative that crypto is primarily a tool for undetectable illicit finance.
insights.quote: some national security officials have described crypto activity as creating “prosecution futures”: transactions recorded now can help investigators identify and prosecute criminals later
insights.locator: Unlike payment methods that may leave no public trace

insights.claim: The authors draw a direct analogy between the 1990s fight over exportable encryption (once classified alongside military technology, later enabling secure banking and ecommerce) and today's debate over blockchain privacy, arguing privacy for legitimate use should be distinguished from secrecy used to evade the law.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Investors should expect the privacy-tooling segment of crypto (mixers, privacy wallets) to face continued political framing battles analogous to 1990s crypto-export wars, with the outcome affecting which privacy tech remains legal to build in the U.S.
insights.locator: The early debate over internet encryption offers a useful comparison

insights.claim: Banks lobbied against stablecoin issuers paying interest on balances because it could pull deposits out of the banking system and reduce loanable funding; CLARITY resolves this by barring interest on stablecoin balances while still permitting transaction-based rewards (e.g., points-like programs for using stablecoins to pay).
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuers and wallet providers should plan product design around transaction-based loyalty/rewards, not yield-on-balance, as the durable legal lane under CLARITY.
insights.locator: Banks have argued that stablecoin issuers and wallet providers

insights.claim: Major incumbent financial institutions — Goldman Sachs, Fidelity, BlackRock, Stripe, Wells Fargo, and JPMorgan — have already built or backed blockchain products, indicating banks see blockchain as shared infrastructure to modernize fragmented financial systems rather than purely a threat.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Named institutional adopters are a concrete watchlist for onchain finance traction; their continued build-out signals institutional demand for CLARITY-style clarity is coming from inside traditional finance, not just crypto-native firms.
insights.locator: Goldman Sachs, Fidelity, BlackRock, Stripe, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan

insights.claim: CLARITY draws a liability line based on intent and participation: developers who knowingly build tools for criminal use or directly assist illegal activity remain liable, but publishers of general-purpose open-source software are not liable for unforeseeable downstream misuse.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: This is a direct read-through to DeFi protocol developers and open-source crypto tooling teams — a settled intent-based liability standard reduces existential legal risk for builders of neutral infrastructure (e.g., mixers, DEX front-ends).
insights.quote: hold people liable when they knowingly facilitate crimes, not when someone later misuses a neutral tool
insights.locator: The workable line is intent and participation

insights.claim: The authors argue unlimited developer liability for downstream misuse would threaten open source software broadly, since it underpins academic research, startups, venture investment, and open AI models, not just crypto.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Frames CLARITY's developer-liability provisions as a precedent relevant beyond crypto, including for open-weight AI model releases — worth tracking as a cross-sector legal precedent.
insights.locator: The consequences would reach far beyond crypto

themes.theme: Risk-based securities framework: SEC to CFTC transition

insights.claim: CLARITY does not exempt tokenized securities from securities law — a tokenized stock remains a stock under SEC oversight regardless of blockchain wrapper.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Removes a bear case that tokenization could be used as a securities-law loophole; tokenized equity platforms should still expect full SEC disclosure/registration requirements.
insights.quote: A tokenized stock is still a stock. It is still a security and remains under SEC oversight.
insights.locator: CLARITY does not turn securities into non-securities

insights.claim: Under CLARITY's risk-based framework, a new blockchain network starting under central control by a founder or small group is treated as a security under SEC oversight with insider disclosure and lockup requirements; once the network meets defined decentralization thresholds, oversight shifts to the CFTC as a commodity, though fraud/manipulation rules still apply.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: This decentralization-threshold mechanism is the single most consequential structural detail for token issuers and early investors — it defines exactly when a project's insider lockups and disclosure burden lift, directly affecting token liquidity timelines and cap-table planning.
insights.locator: A quick summary of CLARITY’s risk-based framework

insights.claim: CLARITY would impose longer lockups and stronger disclosure obligations on founders, venture investors, and other insiders while a network remains centrally controlled, specifically to prevent insiders from selling into the market before it becomes sufficiently decentralized or before the public has comparable information.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: VC-backed token projects should model extended lockup periods into fundraising and exit timelines under a passed CLARITY Act — this is a direct constraint on early-investor liquidity.
insights.locator: Founders, venture investors, and other insiders more broadly

themes.theme: Stakes of inaction and U.S. technological leadership

insights.claim: If CLARITY fails, crypto regulation does not disappear but reverts to fragmented, contestable agency guidance from the SEC, CFTC, and Treasury that can shift between administrations, and the more likely outcome is that companies continue building offshore, where they are harder for U.S. regulators and law enforcement to reach.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Failure of CLARITY is a bearish signal specifically for U.S.-domiciled crypto business formation, not for crypto activity overall — capital and talent migration offshore is the base case absent legislation.
insights.quote: Offshore companies are harder for American regulators to supervise, harder for law enforcement to reach, and less likely to build around U.S. standards.
insights.locator: The industry has survived years of aggressive enforcement

insights.claim: The authors invoke the history of U.S. encryption export restrictions as precedent: when the U.S. restricted strong encryption, foreign competitors kept building it elsewhere and captured the market, and only after restrictions eased did American companies help build the secure internet economy.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: This historical analogy is the authors' core argument for urgency: restrictive or absent U.S. rules don't stop a technology, they just relocate where it's built and who captures the value — directly applicable to where crypto infrastructure investment should be expected to flow.
insights.locator: The history of encryption shows what is at stake

insights.claim: CLARITY has bipartisan congressional backing built over multiple years, and has been endorsed by the Fraternal Order of Police (the largest U.S. law enforcement organization), which has pushed back on claims the bill would weaken sanctions or AML enforcement.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Law enforcement endorsement undercuts the strongest political counter-narrative (that CLARITY enables crime), which is relevant to handicapping the bill's odds of passage.
insights.locator: The Fraternal Order of Police, the country’s largest law enforcement

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has endorsed CLARITY, reflecting broader financial-sector support alongside firms and fintechs already building blockchain products.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A named large-bank CEO endorsement is a concrete data point for tracking institutional political momentum behind the bill's passage odds.
insights.locator: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has endorsed CLARITY
